question.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Life and Personal Liberty?
question.explanation: Article 21 guarantees that no person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except by procedure established by law.

question.question: In which year did Mahatma Gandhi begin the Dandi Salt March?
question.explanation: Mahatma Gandhi launched the Dandi Salt March on 12 March 1930 to protest the British salt monopoly, walking 241 miles to the sea.

question.question: At which venue did Mahatma Gandhi launch the Quit India Movement in 1942?
question.explanation: Gandhi delivered the famous 'Do or Die' speech at Gowalia Tank Maidan in Bombay on 8 August 1942, launching the Quit India Movement.

question.question: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
question.explanation: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume, Dadabhai Naoroji, and Dinshaw Wacha as a platform for Indian political aspirations.

question.question: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India established?
question.explanation: The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and was nationalised in 1949.

question.question: In which year was the Goods and Services Tax (GST) implemented in India?
question.explanation: GST was implemented in India on 1 July 2017, replacing a complex system of indirect taxes with a unified 'one nation one tax' regime.

question.question: On which river is the Hirakud Dam, the longest dam in India, built?
question.explanation: The Hirakud Dam in Odisha is built across the Mahanadi river and, at about 26 km, is the longest earthen dam in the world.

question.question: What is the highest mountain peak in India?
question.explanation: Kanchenjunga (8,586 m) is the highest mountain peak in India, located on the Sikkim-Nepal border, and is the third-highest mountain in the world.

question.question: The classical dance form Bharatanatyam originated in which Indian state?
question.explanation: Bharatanatyam is one of India's oldest classical dance forms, originating in the temples of Tamil Nadu and codified from the Natya Shastra.

question.question: The classical dance-drama Kathakali is the traditional art form of which Indian state?
question.explanation: Kathakali is a highly stylised classical dance-drama from Kerala, renowned for its elaborate costumes, makeup, and enactment of stories from Hindu epics.

question.question: Who is the author of the autobiography Wings of Fire?
question.explanation: Wings of Fire is the autobiography of A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, former President of India and aerospace scientist, co-written with Arun Tiwari and published in 1999.

question.question: Which cell organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
question.explanation: Mitochondria are called the powerhouse of the cell because they generate most of the cell's supply of ATP through the process of cellular respiration.

question.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
question.explanation: Gold's chemical symbol Au comes from the Latin word 'aurum', and it is element number 79 in the periodic table.

question.question: In which year was the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) launched?
question.explanation: PMJDY was launched on 28 August 2014 by Prime Minister Narendra Modi to ensure financial inclusion by providing every household access to a bank account.

question.question: Which is the highest civilian award of India?
question.explanation: Bharat Ratna is the highest civilian honour in India, awarded for exceptional service of the highest order to the nation.

question.question: NITI Aayog replaced which earlier body in 2015?
question.explanation: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) was established on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission which had existed since 1950.

question.question: In which year did the First War of Indian Independence (Sepoy Mutiny) begin?
question.explanation: The Revolt of 1857 began on 10 May 1857 at Meerut and is widely regarded as the First War of Indian Independence against British rule.
question.source_citation: NCERT, Modern India; Britannica, Indian Mutiny

question.question: The Battle of Plassey, which established British supremacy in Bengal, was fought in which year?
question.explanation: The Battle of Plassey was fought on 23 June 1757 between the British East India Company under Robert Clive and Siraj ud-Daulah, marking the foundation of British political rule in India.
question.source_citation: NCERT, Our Pasts III; Britannica, Battle of Plassey

question.question: The Partition of Bengal was carried out by Lord Curzon in which year?
question.explanation: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal on 16 October 1905 on administrative grounds, which sparked a massive nationalist protest and the Swadeshi Movement.
question.source_citation: NCERT, Modern India; Britannica, Partition of Bengal 1905

question.question: In which year did the Jallianwala Bagh massacre take place?
question.explanation: On 13 April 1919, General Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, killing hundreds and deeply radicalising the Indian independence movement.
question.source_citation: NCERT, Modern India; Britannica, Amritsar Massacre

question.question: In which year was the Simon Commission appointed by the British government?
question.explanation: The Simon Commission was constituted in 1927 under Sir John Simon to review the Government of India Act 1919; it was boycotted by Indians because it had no Indian members.
question.source_citation: NCERT, Modern India; Britannica, Simon Commission

question.question: India achieved independence from British rule on which date?
question.explanation: India became an independent nation on 15 August 1947 under the Indian Independence Act 1947, ending nearly 200 years of British rule.

question.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution guarantees the Right to Equality before law?
question.explanation: Article 14 of the Indian Constitution guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to all persons within the territory of India.

question.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution, called the 'Heart and Soul' of the Constitution by Dr. Ambedkar, lets a citizen move the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights?
question.explanation: Article 32 gives citizens the right to move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights, and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution.

question.question: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution can a National Emergency be proclaimed?
question.explanation: Article 352 empowers the President to proclaim a National Emergency if the security of India or any part of it is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion.

question.question: The Fundamental Duties of citizens are enshrined in which Article of the Indian Constitution?
question.explanation: Article 51A, added by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976, lists the Fundamental Duties of every citizen of India.

question.question: Which house of the Indian Parliament is also known as the 'Council of States'?
question.explanation: Rajya Sabha, meaning Council of States, is the upper house of the Indian Parliament and represents the states and union territories of India.
question.source_citation: Constitution of India, Art. 80; Rajya Sabha

question.question: Under which Article of the Indian Constitution can President's Rule be imposed in a state?
question.explanation: Article 356 allows the President to impose President's Rule in a state if the constitutional machinery of that state has failed.

question.question: What is the SI unit of force?
question.explanation: The SI unit of force is the newton (N), defined as the force required to accelerate a mass of one kilogram at one metre per second squared.

question.question: Deficiency of which vitamin causes rickets in children?
question.explanation: Rickets is caused by deficiency of Vitamin D, which is essential for calcium absorption and proper bone mineralisation.

question.question: Which gas is released by green plants during photosynthesis?
question.explanation: During photosynthesis, plants absorb carbon dioxide and water and release oxygen as a by-product when sunlight splits water molecules.

question.question: What is the SI unit of electric current?
question.explanation: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (A), named after French physicist Andre-Marie Ampere.

question.question: What is the atomic number of hydrogen?
question.explanation: Hydrogen has atomic number 1, meaning it has one proton in its nucleus; it is the lightest and most abundant element in the universe.

question.question: Which tree is the National Tree of India?
question.explanation: The Banyan tree (Ficus benghalensis) is the National Tree of India, symbolising longevity and deeply rooted in Indian heritage.

question.question: Which animal is the National Aquatic Animal of India?
question.explanation: The Gangetic River Dolphin (Platanista gangetica) was declared India's National Aquatic Animal in 2009 to promote its conservation.

question.question: On which date is World Environment Day observed every year?
question.explanation: World Environment Day is observed on 5 June every year, established by the United Nations beginning in 1973.

question.question: The classical dance form Manipuri originates from which Indian state?
question.explanation: Manipuri is one of the eight classical dance forms of India, originating from the state of Manipur in the northeastern region.

question.question: Who authored the book 'The Discovery of India'?
question.explanation: The Discovery of India was written by India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru in 1944 while he was imprisoned at Ahmednagar Fort.

question.question: Who was the first woman to serve as President of India?
question.explanation: Pratibha Patil served as the 12th President of India from 2007 to 2012, becoming the first woman to hold the office.

question.question: In which year was the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) given statutory powers through the SEBI Act?
question.explanation: SEBI began in 1988 as a non-statutory body and was accorded statutory powers when the SEBI Act, 1992 came into force on 30 January 1992. The year SEBI became a statutory regulator is a standard banking/SSC GK fact.

question.question: Where is the headquarters of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) located?
question.explanation: SEBI's headquarters is in the Bandra Kurla Complex business district of Mumbai, with regional offices in New Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Ahmedabad. HQ location of regulators is a frequent banking-exam question.

question.question: In which year was the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD) established?
question.explanation: NABARD came into existence on 12 July 1982 as the apex development bank for agriculture and rural development. Its founding year is a high-yield banking and RRB GK fact.

question.question: Where is the headquarters of the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) located?
question.explanation: SIDBI, set up on 2 April 1990 as the apex financial institution for the MSME sector, is headquartered in Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. HQ of SIDBI is a common banking-awareness question.

question.question: Which sector in India is regulated by the IRDAI?
question.explanation: The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) regulates and licenses the insurance and re-insurance industry in India. Matching regulators to their sectors is a staple banking-exam topic.

question.question: Where is the headquarters of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) located?
question.explanation: The RBI's Central Office was originally in Calcutta but was moved to Bombay (Mumbai) in 1937, where its headquarters remains. RBI's HQ is among the most-asked banking GK facts.

question.question: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) nationalised?
question.explanation: Although the RBI was established in 1935 as a shareholders' bank, it was nationalised on 1 January 1949 and has since been fully owned by the Government of India. The nationalisation year is a classic banking-exam distractor against the 1935 founding year.

question.question: What does NITI in 'NITI Aayog' stand for?
distractors: National Institute for Trade and Industry
question.explanation: NITI stands for National Institution for Transforming India, the government's apex public-policy think tank. Acronym full-forms are high-frequency, easy-marks GK questions.

question.question: Which is the longest river flowing within India?
question.explanation: The Ganga, about 2,525 km long, is the longest river in India, rising in the Himalayas and draining into the Bay of Bengal. A perennial favourite in SSC/RRB static-GK river questions.

question.question: Which is the second longest river in India (and longest in peninsular India)?
question.explanation: The Godavari (about 1,465 km) is India's second longest river after the Ganga and the longest of peninsular India, rising at Trimbakeshwar near Nashik, Maharashtra. Commonly asked in SSC/RRB geography.

question.question: Which is the largest Indian state by area?
question.explanation: Rajasthan, at 342,239 sq km (about 10.4% of India's area), is the largest Indian state by area. A high-frequency static-GK fact across SSC, banking and railway exams.

question.question: The Thar Desert (Great Indian Desert) lies mostly in which Indian state?
question.explanation: The majority of the Thar Desert, India's largest desert, lies in Rajasthan, with smaller portions in Gujarat, Haryana and Punjab. A staple SSC/RRB geography fact.

question.question: Which is the largest freshwater lake in India?
question.explanation: Wular Lake, in Jammu and Kashmir and fed by the Jhelum river, is widely cited as India's largest freshwater lake. A frequent static-GK 'largest lake' question in SSC/RRB.
question.source_citation: Wikipedia: Wular Lake; Baramulla District (Govt of India)

question.question: The Bhagirathi, the headstream of the Ganga, rises from which glacier?
question.explanation: The Bhagirathi, the source stream of the Ganga, rises at the snout of the Gangotri Glacier at Gomukh in Uttarakhand. A common river-origin question in SSC/RRB geography.
question.source_citation: Wikipedia: Ganges; NEXT IAS (Ganga River System)

question.question: Which Indian state has the longest coastline?
question.explanation: Gujarat has the longest coastline of any Indian state (about 1,600 km), thanks to the Kathiawar peninsula. A recurring SSC/RRB static-GK fact.

question.question: The Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in India, lies mainly in which state?
question.explanation: The Sundarbans, the world's largest mangrove forest and a UNESCO World Heritage Site home to the Royal Bengal tiger, lies in West Bengal in the Ganges delta. A high-yield SSC/RRB fact.
question.source_citation: Wikipedia: Sundarbans National Park; Ministry of Culture, Govt of India

question.question: Which is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level?
question.explanation: Mount Everest, at 8,848.86 m in the Himalayas on the Nepal-China border, is the highest mountain above sea level on Earth. A foundational world-geography fact in SSC/RRB exams.

question.question: The Lucknow Pact of 1916 was an agreement between the Indian National Congress and which other organization?
question.explanation: Signed at the December 1916 Lucknow session, the pact was a joint scheme of constitutional reform agreed by the Indian National Congress and the All-India Muslim League, and also marked the reunion of the moderate and extremist Congress factions. A high-yield modern-history fact.

question.question: Gandhi's first satyagraha in India, the 1917 Champaran movement in Bihar, was launched against the forced cultivation of which crop?
question.explanation: In Champaran (Bihar), peasants were forced under the teenkathia/tinkathia system to grow indigo for European planters; Gandhi's 1917 intervention was his first satyagraha in India and led to the Champaran Agrarian Act of 1918. Frequently tested as Gandhi's first Indian movement.
question.source_citation: PIB, Government of India / Wikipedia (Champaran Satyagraha)

question.question: Who presided over the 1929 Lahore session of the Indian National Congress, which adopted the Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution?
question.explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru presided over the Lahore session where, on 31 December 1929, the Congress declared Purna Swaraj and fixed 26 January 1930 as the first Independence Day. A staple INC-session question.

question.question: Who presided over the 1931 Karachi session of the Indian National Congress, which passed the resolution on Fundamental Rights and the National Economic Programme?
question.explanation: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel presided over the Karachi session (March 1931), which endorsed the Gandhi-Irwin Pact and adopted the landmark Fundamental Rights resolution (drafted mainly by Nehru). Commonly confused with Nehru, who drafted but did not preside.

question.question: The Poona Pact of 1932, which replaced separate electorates for the Depressed Classes with reserved seats in joint electorates, was signed between Mahatma Gandhi and whom?
question.explanation: Signed on 24 September 1932 at Yerwada Jail after Gandhi's fast against the Communal Award, the Poona Pact between Gandhi and Ambedkar gave the Depressed Classes reserved seats (148) in joint electorates instead of separate electorates. A high-frequency exam fact.

question.question: Which British East India Company commander led the forces that won the Battle of Buxar in 1764?
question.explanation: At Buxar (Oct 1764) Major Hector Munro defeated the combined armies of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Mughal emperor Shah Alam II, paving the way for the Company's Diwani rights in 1765. Robert Clive commanded at Plassey (1757), a common distractor.
question.source_citation: Wikipedia / World History Encyclopedia (Battle of Buxar)

question.question: The Permanent Settlement of 1793, which fixed land revenue and recognised zamindars as proprietors of the soil in Bengal, was introduced by which Governor-General?
question.explanation: Concluded in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis, the Permanent Settlement fixed land revenue in perpetuity for Bengal, Bihar and Orissa and made zamindars hereditary landowners. A high-yield land-revenue-systems question.

question.question: The 1942 British mission that offered India dominion status after World War II, famously called a 'post-dated cheque' by Gandhi, was headed by whom?
question.explanation: Sir Stafford Cripps led the March 1942 mission offering post-war dominion status; Congress rejected it and the failure preceded the Quit India movement. The distractors were members of the later 1946 Cabinet Mission, a common trap.

question.question: Which act abolished dyarchy at the provincial level and introduced provincial autonomy in British India?
question.explanation: The Government of India Act 1935 ended the dyarchy introduced by the 1919 Act in the provinces and granted provincial autonomy, while proposing an all-India federation that never materialised. A frequently tested constitutional milestone.

question.question: The Doctrine of Lapse, used to annex states such as Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur, is associated with which Governor-General?
question.explanation: Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856) applied the Doctrine of Lapse, annexing states like Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur whose rulers died without a natural male heir; the resulting resentment was a key cause of the 1857 revolt. Wellesley is linked instead with the Subsidiary Alliance, a common distractor.

question.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution provides for the constitution of a Finance Commission?
question.explanation: Article 280 empowers the President to constitute a Finance Commission every fifth year to recommend the distribution of tax proceeds between the Union and States; a recurring favourite in SSC/banking polity sections.

question.question: The superintendence, direction and control of elections is vested in the Election Commission under which Article?
question.explanation: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, State legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice-President in the Election Commission; a high-yield constitutional-bodies fact.

question.question: The office of the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India is established under which Article of the Constitution?
question.explanation: Article 148 provides for the CAG, appointed by the President and removable like a Supreme Court judge; commonly asked alongside other constitutional offices.

question.question: Which Article of the Constitution deals with the office of the Attorney-General for India?
question.explanation: Article 76 provides for the Attorney-General, the highest law officer of India, appointed by the President; Article 165 (a distractor) is the parallel office of Advocate-General at the State level.

question.question: The anti-defection law is contained in which Schedule of the Indian Constitution?
question.explanation: The Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment (1985), contains the anti-defection provisions for disqualifying legislators who defect; a frequently tested schedule-mapping fact.

question.question: Which Constitutional Amendment Act is popularly known as the 'Mini-Constitution' for the sweeping changes it made?
question.explanation: The 42nd Amendment (1976), enacted during the Emergency, made extensive changes (added Fundamental Duties, 'Socialist Secular' to the Preamble) earning it the nickname 'Mini-Constitution'; a staple amendments question.

question.question: The Directive Principles of State Policy in the Indian Constitution were borrowed from the Constitution of which country?
question.explanation: The DPSP (Part IV) were inspired by the Irish Constitution (Article 45); contrast with Fundamental Rights from the USA and the parliamentary system from the UK, a classic 'borrowed features' question.
question.source_citation: NCERT Polity / Constitution of India (Part IV)

question.question: Which Article lays down the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and the procedure for it?
question.explanation: Article 368 in Part XX deals with Parliament's constituent power to amend the Constitution by addition, variation or repeal and the procedure therefor; central to the basic-structure doctrine.

question.question: Provisions for the proclamation of a Financial Emergency are contained in which Article of the Constitution?
question.explanation: Article 360 in Part XVIII empowers the President to declare a Financial Emergency if India's financial stability or credit is threatened; never invoked, and tested against National (352) and President's Rule (356) emergencies.

question.question: The list of officially recognised languages of India is given in which Schedule of the Constitution?
question.explanation: The Eighth Schedule lists the officially recognised languages (currently 22, up from the original 14); commonly confused with the Seventh (Union/State/Concurrent lists) and Tenth (anti-defection) Schedules.
question.source_citation: Constitution of India (Eighth Schedule) / Ministry of Home Affairs

question.question: The Ranji Trophy, India's premier domestic championship, is associated with which sport?
question.explanation: The Ranji Trophy is India's annual domestic first-class cricket championship, organised by the BCCI and named after Ranjitsinhji. Trophy-to-sport associations are staple GK in SSC and bank exams.

question.question: The Thomas Cup is the world men's team championship in which sport?
question.explanation: The Thomas Cup is the international men's team badminton championship run by the Badminton World Federation. Cup-to-sport pairings appear regularly in static GK sections.

question.question: Which is India's highest wartime military gallantry award?
question.explanation: The Param Vir Chakra is the highest military decoration awarded for valour during wartime, ranking above the Maha Vir Chakra and Vir Chakra. The order of gallantry awards is a frequent exam topic.
question.source_citation: Wikipedia / National War Memorial (Govt. of India)

question.entity: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
question.question: Which is the highest sporting honour of India?
question.answer: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
question.explanation: The Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award is India's highest sporting honour, given for outstanding performance over four years; it ranks above the Arjuna Award. National sports awards and their hierarchy are core static GK.

question.question: Which award is the second-highest sporting honour of India, given for outstanding performance in sports?
distractors: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
question.explanation: Instituted in 1961, the Arjuna Award is the second-highest sporting honour (after the Khel Ratna), given to sportspersons for outstanding performance. Awards and their precedence recur in SSC/bank GK.

question.question: Which national award is given to outstanding sports coaches in India?
distractors: Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna Award
question.explanation: Instituted in 1985, the Dronacharya Award honours coaches whose trainees excel in international events, unlike the Arjuna and Khel Ratna awards given to players. Award-purpose questions are common in exams.

question.question: How many players from each team are on the court at the start of a standard kabaddi match?
question.explanation: In standard team kabaddi, two teams of seven players each occupy opposite halves of the court. Number-of-players-per-team facts are frequent static GK items.

question.question: The Santosh Trophy, an inter-state national competition in India, is associated with which sport?
question.explanation: The Santosh Trophy is India's inter-state national football competition contested under the All India Football Federation. Trophy-to-sport associations are reliable exam fodder.

question.question: The Davis Cup is the premier international team event in which sport?
question.explanation: The Davis Cup is the premier international men's team tennis competition, often called the 'World Cup of Tennis'. Cup-to-sport links are standard static GK.

question.question: How many players, including the goalkeeper, make up a field hockey team on the pitch?
question.explanation: Under the FIH Rules of Hockey, each field hockey team consists of eleven players on the pitch (ten outfield players and one goalkeeper). Players-per-team counts are common exam questions.

question.question: The PFRDA is the statutory body that regulates which of the following in India?
question.explanation: The Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority (PFRDA) is the statutory regulator for pensions in India, overseeing schemes such as the National Pension System (NPS) and Atal Pension Yojana. Regulator-to-sector matching is high-yield for banking exams.

question.question: By total geographical area, which is the tiniest state in India?
question.explanation: Goa, covering just 3,702 sq km, is India's smallest state by area. Frequently paired with 'largest state' questions in SSC/RRB static GK.
